question_text: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police. The patient was found intoxicated at a local bar. The patient is combative and smells of alcohol. The patient has a past medical history of alcoholism, IV drug use, and schizophrenia. His current medications include IM haloperidol and ibuprofen. The patient is currently homeless and has presented to the emergency department similarly multiple times. His temperature is 97.0°F (36.1°C), blood pressure is 130/87 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, respirations are 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Physical exam is deferred due to patient non-compliance. Laboratory values reveal an acute kidney injury and a normal PT/PTT. The patient is started on IV fluids and ketorolac to control symptoms of a headache. The patient begins to vomit into a basin. The nursing staff calls for help when the patient’s vomit appears grossly bloody. Which of the following best describes the most likely diagnosis?

                    ### Question
                    A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police. The patient was found intoxicated at a local bar. The patient is combative and smells of alcohol. The patient has a past medical history of alcoholism, IV drug use, and schizophrenia. His current medications include IM haloperidol and ibuprofen. The patient is currently homeless and has presented to the emergency department similarly multiple times. His temperature is 97.0°F (36.1°C), blood pressure is 130/87 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, respirations are 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Physical exam is deferred due to patient non-compliance. Laboratory values reveal an acute kidney injury and a normal PT/PTT. The patient is started on IV fluids and ketorolac to control symptoms of a headache. The patient begins to vomit into a basin. The nursing staff calls for help when the patient’s vomit appears grossly bloody. Which of the following best describes the most likely diagnosis?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Dilated submucosal esophageal veins
opb. Gastric mucosal erosion
opc. Mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction
opd. Transmural distal esophagus tear
ope. Transmural erosion of the gastric wall

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The most likely diagnosis for the patient presenting with grossly bloody vomit is a mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction, known as a Mallory-Weiss tear. This is supported by the chain: 'Alcohol intoxication' leads to 'vomiting,' which increases 'intra-abdominal pressure,' resulting in a 'mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction,' causing 'grossly bloody vomit.' This aligns with the standard medical consensus that Mallory-Weiss tears are common in patients with a history of alcohol use and vomiting. The retrieved evidence path supports the link between alcohol intoxication and vomiting, which is a key factor in the development of a Mallory-Weiss tear. Other options, such as dilated submucosal esophageal veins (esophageal varices), are less likely given the acute presentation and lack of severe portal hypertension signs. Gastric mucosal erosion and transmural tears are also less consistent with the clinical picture and typical presentation of acute bloody vomiting in this context.
